climbing_route.label: West saddle to the summit pinnacle
climbing_route.notes: From the basin climb to the saddle on the peak's west side, then traverse/scramble east and around to approach the summit pinnacle from its south side; sustained on talus and blocky rock, with loose rock and sliding scree. The described line tops out at the base of the summit block itself, at 6,971 ft, where the roped climbing begins — the summit block climbing is not described.

climbing_route.label: Southwest ridge from Kangaroo Pass
climbing_route.notes: At Kangaroo Pass (6,671 ft) leave the boot path and turn northeast onto Wallaby Peak's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail continues briefly then disappears on rock; stay on or near the ridge crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree, and grassy benches.

climbing_route.label: South-facing summit gully
climbing_route.notes: At about 7,400 ft swing around onto the south flank into the south-facing summit gully. Moderately steep with notable loose rock and scree — wear a helmet, especially with more than one person in the party, since climbers above can kick debris down onto those below; some parties pick a short Class 3 line on the gully's margins to avoid the worst of the scree.

climbing_route.label: Exit left to the true summit
climbing_route.notes: Near the top of the gully, exit left (northeast) for the short final scramble to the true summit. Budget about an hour pass-to-summit.

climbing_route.label: Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass
climbing_route.notes: From Whatcom Pass leave the trail and climb/contour south and east to gain the Whatcom Glacier at roughly 5,200-5,500 ft; rope up for glacier travel toward Perfect Pass, the notch/saddle south of the peak. Crevasses and moats open through the season, and the surface can go from soft névé early on to bare, polished ice with exposed water channels by mid-to-late summer.

climbing_route.label: South-facing summit snowfield
climbing_route.notes: From the glacier's high point near Perfect Pass, ascend the broad south-facing snowfield below the summit.

climbing_route.label: South ridge crest to the top
climbing_route.notes: Finish on an exposed but moderate scramble along the south ridge crest to the top.

climbing_route.label: Col to the summit shoulder via the west ridge (Option A)
climbing_route.notes: From the meadow basin at about 6,100 ft trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder. Trail-less with route-finding and loose talus/scree in the gullies, and real exposure near the ridge crest; early-season snow can make the gully sections firm or icy.

climbing_route.label: Final rock gully and headwall ramp
climbing_route.notes: The final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above.

climbing_route.label: South ridge from 6,180 ft (Option B)
climbing_route.notes: Intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft, then scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; loose talus/scree in the gullies and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully.

climbing_route.label: Southwest slopes variant
climbing_route.notes: Alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (north) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way.

wa_white_mountain_olympics_scramble.skip_reason: The approach text describes only the two hikes in and stops at camp: it ends "camping at Marmot Lake (established site, toilet, bear wire) at the base of White Mountain's south buttresses" (and, on the north side, at "Honeymoon Meadows camp (~mile 15, established campsite)"). Nothing above camp — no scramble terrain, direction, or class — is described.

climbing_route.label: Continuous snow/ice on the shoulder and face
climbing_route.notes: Climbed roughly April–June as an early-season snow/ice ascent while the couloirs, glacier basin, and connecting slopes are still fully snow-covered corn/névé; parties stay on continuous snow/ice higher on the shoulder and face rather than threading the rock bands that appear once the snowpack recedes. Many skin/boot the glacier basin on skis or splitboards. Expect firmer early-morning snow requiring a timed start, and real avalanche hazard in the entry couloir and on the glacier headwall that isn't a factor once the route melts out later in the year — check the NWAC forecast and go when the freeze-thaw cycle is consolidating the snowpack, not loading it.

climbing_route.label: Final steep pitch below the summit
climbing_route.notes: Parties switch to crampons only for the final steep pitch below the summit.
